title: The Courier in the Drifts
subtitle: Three Herrings, a Strongbox, and Somebody Half-Dead in the Pass

setting.name: The Undercroft, the Yard, and the First Half-Mile of the Pass
setting.description: Days five and six. The House has convicted Corwin Tace by general agreement and nobody has said so out loud. The party's welcome has run out: doors that were open on day two are shut on day five, and the people who still talk to them are the ones nobody else talks to either. Downstairs, the bursar's counting-room and a strongbox with three letters in it. Outside in the yard, a postern door, a woodpile and a set of prints that everybody has decided belong to an intruder. And beyond the wall, in the first half-mile of Coldharrow Pass, something comes most of the way up on the fifth afternoon and does not arrive.
setting.atmosphere: Cold gone social. The House is not hostile — it is worse than that; it is polite in the particular way that means a decision has been taken about you. Conversations end when the party enters a room. The cook is short. The journeymen eat fast. And then, on the fifth afternoon, all of that stops mattering for four hours because there is a man in the drifts and the House becomes, briefly and completely, twelve people doing the right thing very well together, which is the memory the party will carry out of this building.

keyLocations.name: The Bursar's Counting-Room
keyLocations.description: Off the undercroft: a desk, a candle, tally books going back forty years, and an iron strongbox let into the wall with a good lock on it. Corwin Tace spends most of days five and six in here with the door shut.
features: A strongbox with a good lock — DC 15 with thieves' tools, and it is not a trap, only a lock
Forty years of tally books, one of which has an entry for the night of the death written up in an hour's worth of sequence
Three letters from a grain factor in the eastern hundreds, folded small, at the bottom under the House's silver
encounters: Tace, who has stopped eating at the long table and takes bread down here instead
The strongbox, which can be opened by lock, by pressure on Tace, or by Oriel Fenn's memory of letters that did not go in the House bag
The tally book, which is Tace's own alibi and which he will not produce
secrets: C7: three letters promising Tace a share on 'early-frost purchases' against advance sight of the tables. Real, criminal, and not the murder
The entry Tace was writing at nine o'clock on the second night is a falsification of the House's flour account, and it takes an hour to write up, and it is why he was in the undercroft

keyLocations.name: The Yard and the Postern
keyLocations.description: The woodpile under its lean-to, the mule shed, the laundry door, and the postern in the wall giving onto the open hill. In the snow: prints going out and coming back, twice, which the House has decided belong to somebody who came in from outside.
features: A postern that is barred at night and was found unbarred on the morning after the death, because a sixteen-year-old forgot
Prints from the kitchen door to the woodpile and back, twice, on the night of the second
Beyond the wall, untrodden snow to the limit of sight, and a pass that is six feet deep and impassable
encounters: Jory Pike, who will lie about the second wood trip badly and look terrible doing it
Oriel Fenn, who will lie for him and stop the moment she believes he is safe
The tracks themselves, which disprove H3 completely to anyone who reads them properly
secrets: No track leads TO the postern from beyond the wall. All of them lead from the woodpile. There was no intruder and there could not have been one
The log tally in the undercroft records two trips that evening, which matches the boy exactly

keyLocations.name: The First Half-Mile of the Pass
keyLocations.description: Beyond the yard wall, where the ground drops away into the pass proper. Six feet of drift, a wind that takes the breath out of a person in twenty minutes, and — on the fifth afternoon — a shape in it that is not a rock.
features: Drift deep enough to swallow a person standing upright, over broken ground nobody can see
A wind that makes ropes mandatory and shouting useless
A courier from the village of Ambry Vale who has got two-thirds of the way up and stopped
encounters: The rescue: set-piece two of three in the entire campaign, and it is against weather rather than a creature
The wolves, if the party goes late and unlucky
Getting him back over the wall alive
secrets: The courier came up because the village has heard nothing from the House and the printer has written twice. He carries the printer's second letter and it names a date: the fair copy must be at the press within eleven days of thaw
He will lose two fingers and he will live, and what he has to say when he can speak changes the harvest thread's clock

keyLocations.name: The Long Table, Day Six
keyLocations.description: Breakfast on the sixth morning with a rescued man upstairs, a bursar who has not appeared for two days, and a House that has to decide out loud what it thinks. The scenario's social climax.
features: Twelve residents, the party, and one empty chair
The first open argument the House has had since the death
Merrit Doane, saying Tace's name in front of everybody for the fourth day running
encounters: The House turning on Tace in the open, and the party's choice about whether to let it
Oriel Fenn giving Tace's alibi at last, unprompted, because she has decided the boy is safe
Ilsabet Wray, saying nothing, being visibly relieved, and hating it
secrets: Fenn's alibi for Tace is the disproof of H1 and it has been available since day three to anyone who asked her properly in her own kitchen
Wray's relief is the single most readable thing she does in the entire campaign and it lasts about two seconds

synopsis: By the fifth day the House has convicted the bursar by general agreement and the party's welcome has run out. This is the scenario of the three herrings: Corwin Tace, who is guilty of selling advance sight of the tables to a grain factor and will lie about every hour of the evening to keep that shut; Pell Oduya, whose bloodied sleeve was a nosebleed at supper that three people watched; and the intruder at the postern, who was a sixteen-year-old fetching wood. Each is real, each is disprovable, and each costs the party time they cannot spare. In the middle of it, on the fifth afternoon, a courier from the village gets two-thirds of the way up the pass and stops — and for four hours the House stops being a room full of suspects and becomes twelve people doing something difficult extremely well together. He lives. What he carries changes the clock on the harvest, and by the sixth morning there are two days left and the party has eliminated three people and named nobody.
hook: You notice it at breakfast on the fifth morning and it takes you a moment to work out what has changed, because nothing has: the same people, the same porridge, the same low argument about a decimal. Then you realise that the argument stopped when you came in and started again when you sat down, and that it started again about something else. Nobody is rude. Nobody looks at you. Halva Onn says good morning. Oriel Fenn puts the dish down at your end without a word and takes it away again ten minutes later, and there is a chair at the far end that has been empty for two days because the bursar has stopped coming up. And Merrit Doane, from the middle of the table, into a silence, for the fourth morning running: 'Well, somebody should say it. He hasn't eaten with us since Tuesday.'

acts.title: Act 1: Three Wrong Answers
acts.description: The herrings, worked through in order, each of them costing time and goodwill. This act is the campaign's engine: the party spends two days eliminating people and ends up with fewer suspects and no answer.
objectives: Get into Tace's strongbox, or get Tace to talk, and find the grain factor's letters (C7)
Read the tracks in the yard and establish there was no intruder
Notice that eliminating three people has not produced a fourth

scenes.name: The Strongbox
scenes.description: C7. Three letters, a real crime, and the wrong crime. The party can reach them by lock, by pressure, or by the cook.
scenes.readAloud: "The counting-room is warm because Tace has been living in it, and it smells of candle and old paper and a man who has not been upstairs for two days. Forty years of tally books on the shelf. A desk with a blotter and a half-eaten heel of bread on it. And in the wall, a strongbox of about a foot square with a lock in it that somebody paid proper money for, sixty years ago, when this House still had money to pay for locks. Under the House's silver, folded small and pushed to the back where a hand would have to go looking, there are three letters. They are from a grain factor at Marrowby in the eastern hundreds. They are addressed to Corwin Tace personally. And the first line of the third one begins: 'Friend — the early-frost purchases went off well again and I enclose your share as before, with thanks for the sight of the tables in good time.'"

skillChecks.success: The lock is a good one and old and you have it in about two minutes with the right tools. It is a lock and nothing else; there is no trap, no alarm and no second mechanism, because this is a house of arithmetic and not a dungeon.
skillChecks.failure: You cannot get it, or you get it and mark it, and Tace knows within a day and becomes an enemy rather than a coward for the rest of the campaign.

skillChecks.success: Tace, who believes he is about to be hanged for a murder, will hand you the letters himself rather than let you look for a motive he has not got. He does it in a rush, badly, and then sits down on the floor of his own counting-room.
skillChecks.failure: He shuts the door in your face and does not open it again, and the strongbox stays shut, and the House hears about it by supper.

skillChecks.success: ALTERNATE ROUTE: Oriel Fenn, in her kitchen, asked properly. 'He's had letters he didn't put in the House bag. Three or four this year. I'd know, because I do the bag.' That does not open the box, but it tells the party exactly what is in it and gives them the lever to make Tace open it himself.
skillChecks.failure: The cook is short with you today and everybody is short with you today and you have not earned anything in this kitchen.

scenes.roleplayNotes: C7 must land as a genuine crime and a complete dead end at the same time. Tace sold advance sight of the eastern tables to a grain factor who bought cheap on the strength of a frost date. He took money for it. He is finished when it comes out. And he did not kill anybody, and did not know Ardwen had found the falsification, and the falsification is not even his — he was profiting from somebody else's error without knowing it was an error. That last detail is worth giving to a party who asks the right follow-up.
loot: C7: three letters from a grain factor at Marrowby promising Tace a share on early-frost purchases

scenes.name: An Hour in the Undercroft
scenes.description: Tace's alibi, which is airtight, which he will not use, and which Oriel Fenn has been sitting on since day three because nobody asked her the right question.
scenes.readAloud: "He does not fight it. That is the thing that finally convinces you. You put the three letters on his own desk in front of him and he looks at them for a while and then he says, 'Yes,' and then he says, 'And I did not touch him,' and then, with the particular exhaustion of a man who has been holding two entirely different lies in his head for four days: 'I was down here. From nine until the alarm. Writing up the flour account.' A pause. 'Writing it up wrong. Which is why I have spent four days letting this House think I killed a man, because the other thing I would have had to explain was that.'"

skillChecks.success: The entry is there in the tally book in his hand and it is an hour's worth of sequence — forty lines of running totals that cannot be written in five minutes and cannot be back-dated without showing. Whatever else he is, he was down here.
skillChecks.failure: A page of figures in a tally book. You would need a reckoner to tell you how long it took to write.

skillChecks.success: Oriel Fenn confirms it flatly the moment you ask her the right question, which is not 'did Tace do it' but 'who went past your kitchen and when.' 'He went down at nine. I heard him under my floor while I set the bread. He came up at ten, near enough, and then the boy started screaming.'
skillChecks.failure: 'I'm not talking about that man in my kitchen.'

skillChecks.success: He is not relieved to be cleared of the murder. He is calculating what happens to him at thaw now that the letters are out, and the answer is that he is ruined and knows it, and he would genuinely rather have been suspected for another three days.
skillChecks.failure: A frightened man who has stopped lying.

scenes.roleplayNotes: H1 disproved. This should feel like a loss rather than a win: the party has spent two days and most of their remaining welcome to eliminate the person everybody was sure about, and there are three days left. Tace's ruin is real and permanent and the party has caused it and it was necessary, and the DM should let that be uncomfortable without moralising about it.

scenes.name: Blood and Snow
scenes.description: H2 and H3 together, both disproved in an afternoon by people the party has been kind to. Fast, and deliberately anticlimactic.
scenes.readAloud: "It takes about an hour, in the end, and the whole time you are doing it you are aware of how much of the week you have already lost. The sleeve: Nan Gaddy has had it in her wash since the third and says, without being asked twice, that it is a nosebleed and that Pell Oduya has had them all winter and that she saw this one happen at the supper table. Two journeymen say the same. And the yard: you go out with a lantern and you read the snow properly for the first time, and everything about it is wrong for an intruder and exactly right for a boy fetching wood — every track runs kitchen door to woodpile to kitchen door, twice, and beyond the wall there is nothing at all, not a mark, out to the limit of what a lantern will show, over ground that no living thing has crossed since the storm."

skillChecks.success: H2 disproved. The blood in the sleeve dried hours before the death and was laundered afterwards; the pattern is a nosebleed's, from above, and not a blow's.
skillChecks.failure: Blood is blood and this shirt has been washed.

skillChecks.success: H3 disproved. No track leads to the postern from beyond the wall. Everything runs from the woodpile, twice, in a boy's boots, and the drift beyond the yard has not been crossed by anything.
skillChecks.failure: Snow, a great many prints, and a postern that was found unbarred. It still looks like somebody came in.

skillChecks.success: Jory Pike admits the second wood trip once he is convinced nobody is going to hang him for it, which takes about four minutes and requires Oriel Fenn to be in the room and on the party's side. The log tally matches him exactly.
skillChecks.failure: The boy lies about it again, worse, and the cook puts herself between him and the party and that is the end of the conversation.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Run both disproofs quickly and let the anticlimax do the work. Three herrings, three real explanations, no murderer, and three days left. If the party is now stuck, this is the point where the DM should let them notice that they have never once asked the old man by the fire what he heard.

acts.title: Act 2: Something in the Pass
acts.description: Set-piece two of three: a courier from the village two-thirds of the way up the pass, in the drifts, in a wind, at four in the afternoon with the light going. There is no enemy in this act at all. It is the best hour the House has and the party should be part of it.
objectives: Get to the courier before dark
Get him back over the wall alive
Keep everyone who went out from becoming a second casualty
Learn what he came up to say

scenes.name: A Shape That Is Not a Rock
scenes.description: Wat Ormery sees it from the yard wall at about four. Then the House moves, all at once, competently, without argument, and it is the first thing everybody has agreed on in five days.
scenes.readAloud: "Wat Ormery has gone up onto the yard wall for no reason at all, the way he does twice a day, and he stands there rather longer than usual, and then he says — not loudly, in the voice of a man who has already started counting rope — 'There's someone in the pass.' And then this building, which has spent five days being twelve people who cannot look at each other, turns into something else entirely in about ninety seconds. Fenn is filling stone bottles with hot water. Gaddy is stripping the drying loft of every blanket on the line. Onn has the rope-store open. Ormery is knotting a line and passing it over his shoulder without stopping to explain, and Ysobel Kirren, who is four foot eleven and weighs nothing, is already in the yard with her coat on, because somebody light has to go first over ground that will not hold."

skillChecks.success: You read the drift and pick a line that will hold weight, and you get to him in forty minutes instead of two hours, which is the whole difference for a man who has been down since noon.
skillChecks.failure: You take the direct line and it is not the right one; somebody goes in to the chest and has to be dug out, and you reach him after dark. He loses two fingers instead of one and the party is out there for another hour.

skillChecks.success: You get him up out of the drift and onto the rope. He is a dead weight, and the wind is taking your breath, and it is the hardest physical thing anyone has done since the pass.
skillChecks.failure: You cannot lift him alone in that footing and it takes three of you and twenty minutes: DC 12 Constitution save for everyone on the rope or gain a level of exhaustion.

skillChecks.success: You get him warm the right way — slowly, out of the wind, no fire and no spirits — and he keeps eight fingers and his life. Aldous Penn will follow anyone who does this correctly for the rest of the campaign.
skillChecks.failure: He lives. He loses two fingers to the frost and there is nothing anyone could have done about it in that wind, which is true and does not help.

enemies: 3 wolves (only if the party goes out after full dark, or leaves the courier unattended on the return)
combatEncounters.tactics: Optional and avoidable. The pack that trailed the party up the pass in rh-scenario-001 has been living on the hill and will investigate a stationary warm body at dusk. They will not press an attack against a group with lights and rope, and they break off after one round of real resistance. If the party handled the wolves well on the road up, they may recognise individuals, which is a nice beat. Do not turn this into a fight if it can be a threat.
combatEncounters.terrain: Drift to chest height over broken ground, in a wind that reduces visibility to thirty feet and makes shouted communication impossible. Everyone should be roped. Difficult terrain throughout; any character who goes in to the chest is restrained until pulled free.

scenes.roleplayNotes: THIS IS THE HOUSE AT ITS BEST AND THE PLAYERS SHOULD SEE IT. Twelve people who have spent five days suspecting each other move as one unit, without argument, without hierarchy, each doing the thing they are good at, because there is a man in the snow. Give every named resident one thing to do. Ilsabet Wray is out there on the rope with everybody else and she is very good at it, and the party should register that and not know what to do with it.

scenes.name: What He Came to Say
scenes.description: The courier, warm, upstairs, at about nine that night, able to talk. He changes the clock on the harvest thread.
scenes.readAloud: "He is about twenty-five and he is from the village and his name is Ewan Barr, and by nine that night he is upright in the loft under six blankets with his hands wrapped, and he has been trying to talk for an hour and been told to shut up by four different people. Now they let him. 'Printer's written twice,' he says. 'Village had nothing from the House since first frost and the press is booked. He says —' and he stops, and starts again, because his mouth is not working properly yet, '— he says the fair copy has to be at the press within eleven days of thaw or he can't set it, and he's got the errata sheet in the letter, and he wants to know whether he's setting that too, and nobody's answered him, and my mother said someone had to come up.'"

skillChecks.success: He is not carrying a message about the murder. Nobody in the village knows there has been a death; nobody could. Whatever is happening in this House is still entirely contained in this House and will be until thaw.
skillChecks.failure: A half-frozen man delivering a message about a printer.

skillChecks.success: The printer's letter names the errata sheet explicitly, which means the printer knows it exists, which means at least one other person outside this building knows there was something wrong with the eastern tables. That is a weapon and the party should recognise it as one.
skillChecks.failure: A letter about a press and a deadline.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The courier's arrival does three things: it proves the pass is impassable (a fit young man got two-thirds of the way and nearly died), it puts a hard date on the harvest thread, and it hands the party the fact that the printer knows. It does not bring help, it does not bring news, and it does not open the pass. Do not let the players hope it will.
loot: The printer's second letter: eleven days from thaw, and a direct question about whether the errata sheet is to be set

acts.title: Act 3: The Sixth Morning
acts.description: Breakfast on the sixth day. The House has to say out loud what it thinks, Tace's alibi comes out at the long table, and for about two seconds Ilsabet Wray is the most readable person in the building.
objectives: Let the House have its argument, or intervene in it
Hear Oriel Fenn clear Tace in front of everybody
Watch the room when the suspicion moves
Arrive at day seven with three people eliminated and nobody named

scenes.name: Somebody Should Say It
scenes.description: The first open argument the House has had since the death, at the long table, with everyone present. The scenario's social climax and its most important two seconds.
scenes.readAloud: "It is Merrit Doane who starts it, at breakfast, for the fifth morning running, and this time nobody stops him. 'He has not eaten with us since Tuesday. He has been in that counting-room with the door shut for four days. He was the only one of us with anything to gain and everybody in this room knows it and nobody will say it, so I am saying it.' And into the pause that follows — before the party can speak, before anyone can — Oriel Fenn puts a dish down rather harder than she needs to and says: 'He went down to the cellar at nine and he was under my kitchen floor till ten and I heard him the whole time, and I have been waiting five days for one of you to ask me instead of deciding. So no. Not him.' And there is a silence of a particular quality. And in it, at the middle of the table, Ilsabet Wray closes her eyes for about two seconds and lets out a breath."

skillChecks.success: You see it. Two seconds, in a room where everybody is reacting to something, and one person reacts to the wrong thing: relief, unmistakable and immediate, on the face of the senior computer — and then, half a second later, something much worse arriving on top of it.
skillChecks.failure: A room full of people reacting to a bombshell at breakfast. You could not pick a single face out of it.

skillChecks.success: If you caught the breath: that was not the relief of an innocent person hearing a friend cleared. It was the relief of someone who had been letting it happen, and the thing that landed on top of it was shame. Note it and say nothing at this table.
skillChecks.failure: Somebody is relieved that Tace is cleared. Most people are.

skillChecks.success: You keep the room from turning on the next person immediately, which it is about to, and which would cost the party the seventh day entirely.
skillChecks.failure: The table decides within ninety seconds that if it was not Tace it was one of the outsiders, and says so, and it is a very bad breakfast.

scenes.roleplayNotes: THE TWO SECONDS ARE THE POINT OF THE WHOLE SCENARIO. A DC 15 Perception at a breakfast table is the first thing in the campaign that points at Ilsabet Wray, and if it is missed there is no alternate route to it — it is a moment and not a clue, it does not appear in the caseFile's clue list, and the party can still reach the truth entirely through C3, C8 and the timeline. If it is caught, do not confirm anything: a player who says 'it was Wray' at this table gets an ordinary, tired, slightly puzzled woman looking back at them, and no confession, and six residents who now think the outsiders are flailing.

scenes.name: Two Days
scenes.description: The end of the scenario: an accounting, out loud, of what the party has and what is left.
scenes.readAloud: "Two days. That is what it comes to when you sit down after breakfast and count it, and it is a very short number. Two days until the couriers come up and the riders come with them and this stops being yours. What you have: a man who was struck from behind and then arranged at the foot of a stair. A lamp that never came down. A weight on the wrong hook. A coat that belongs to one of three people. Three years of tables signed by one hand twice, and two hundred years of observations that say the instrument was never wrong. What you do not have is anybody at the top of that stair at a quarter past nine — and the three people you were certain about have all been cleared by other people's honest evidence, which is somehow worse than if they were still suspects."
scenes.roleplayNotes: End the scenario with an explicit, honest inventory. In a mystery the DM should periodically say aloud what the party has established, because the players are tracking twelve names across six sessions and it is not a failure of play to lose the thread. List the clues held, name the three eliminated, and state the days remaining. Then stop. Do not hint at what is missing.

npcsInvolved.name: Corwin Tace, 47
npcsInvolved.description: Guilty of selling advance sight of the eastern tables to a grain factor at Marrowby and taking a share on the purchases. Innocent of the murder, with an airtight alibi he would not use because using it meant explaining what he was doing in the undercroft. Ruined the moment the letters come out, and knows it, and would genuinely have preferred another three days of being suspected of killing a man.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the strongbox shut. That is the whole of it, and it has cost him everything, and he did not kill anybody.

npcsInvolved.name: Oriel Fenn, 52
npcsInvolved.description: Has known Tace's alibi since the night it happened and has been waiting five days for somebody to ask her the right question, which is not 'did he do it' but 'who went past your kitchen and when.' She gives it at the long table on the sixth morning because she has decided Jory Pike is safe and she no longer needs to keep everybody out of her kitchen.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Twelve people fed three times a day, the boy protected, and nobody deciding things in her kitchen.

npcsInvolved.name: Jory Pike, 16
npcsInvolved.description: Went out the postern for wood twice on the night of the death, as he does every evening, and left the prints the House has decided belong to an intruder. Lies about the second trip, badly, because he forgot to bar the postern and is certain that is what killed the Master. Frightened, honest, and entirely protected by the cook.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To not be blamed for a door.

npcsInvolved.name: Pell Oduya, 29
npcsInvolved.description: Nosebleed at supper, sleeve marked, quarrel with the Master in front of witnesses forty minutes before he died, and an alibi from two other journeymen that he will produce immediately because he has nothing to hide and is terrified anyway. He gets worse the more he is questioned, which is normal and means nothing.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To not be humiliated in front of the House twice.

npcsInvolved.name: Ewan Barr, 25
npcsInvolved.description: Came up because the village has heard nothing since first frost and the printer has written twice, and got two-thirds of the way. Loses one or two fingers depending on how well the rescue goes. Carries the printer's second letter, which names the errata sheet and puts eleven days from thaw on the fair copy.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His mother said somebody had to go up. He does not know there has been a death and will not for another day.

npcsInvolved.name: Wat Ormery, 45
npcsInvolved.description: Sees the shape from the yard wall and has rope over his shoulder before he has finished the sentence. Will not attempt the pass himself and is completely right not to, and the difference between that and going out half a mile for a man he can see is the difference between sense and cowardice, and he knows exactly where the line is.

npcsInvolved.name: Ilsabet Wray, 54
npcsInvolved.description: Out on the rope in the drifts with everybody else on the fifth afternoon, and very good at it. Silent through the sixth morning's argument, and relieved for about two seconds when Tace is cleared, and then not relieved at all. This is the first moment in the campaign that points at her and it is a moment rather than a clue.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Not money. She signed off three years of eastern frost tables without checking the reduction, out of overwork and pride, and Ardwen's errata sheet would have bound the House's negligence and her signature into an Almanac that every farm keeps on a nail for a year. She went up to ask him to hold it one season; he refused; she picked up the weight. She had no plan and has no second one. She will not let anyone else hang, but she will let them be suspected, and she is finding out this week exactly how much of that she can stand.

npcsInvolved.name: Merrit Doane, 22
npcsInvolved.description: Says Tace's name at breakfast for the fifth morning running and is publicly, comprehensively wrong in front of the whole House. He does not apologise and he does not stop; he simply moves to a new name within a day, and the DM should let him move to whichever name the party has been asking about most.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To have been right about something for a man who is dead.

rewards.gold: None. Ewan Barr has four shillings and a printer's letter. The House's silver is in Tace's strongbox and belongs to the House.
items: C7 — three letters from a grain factor at Marrowby, promising Tace a share on early-frost purchases against advance sight of the tables
The printer's second letter: the fair copy must be at the press within eleven days of thaw, and does the House intend the errata sheet to be set?
Corwin Tace's tally book entry, an hour's worth of sequence, which is his alibi and his fraud in the same forty lines
The log tally recording two wood trips on the night of the death
rewards.story: Three herrings, three real explanations, and nobody named. The bursar is cleared and ruined; the journeyman's sleeve was a nosebleed three people watched; the intruder at the postern was a sixteen-year-old fetching wood and forgetting to bar a door. A courier nearly died in the pass and did not, and what he carried put eleven days from thaw on a fair copy that still has three years of false frost dates in it. Two days left, three people eliminated, and — for anyone who was watching the right face at breakfast — two seconds of relief on the sixth morning that do not belong to an innocent person.

twists: Tace's alibi has been available since the third day from the cook, and nobody asked her, because everybody asked her whether he did it instead of asking her who went past her kitchen. The best witness in a closed house is the person who was working.

Tace would rather have been suspected of murder for another three days than have three letters read aloud, and says so, and means it. He is ruined by the party's investigation and he is not the murderer, and both of those things are permanent.

The rescue in the pass is the House at its absolute best: twelve people who have spent five days suspecting each other moving as one unit without argument, because there is a man in the snow. Ilsabet Wray is out there on the rope and she is very good at it.
The courier proves the pass is a wall rather than a delay: a fit young man went two-thirds of the way and nearly died, and there is no help coming and there never was.

The first thing in the entire campaign to point at Ilsabet Wray is not a clue. It is two seconds at a breakfast table on the sixth morning, available on a DC 15 Perception, with no alternate route, and the party can still reach the truth without it.
dmTips: RUN ALL THREE HERRINGS TO A CLEAN CONCLUSION IN THIS SCENARIO. Their disproofs are in the caseFile and every one of them comes from a person the party has either been kind to or has not — Oriel Fenn for Tace, Nan Gaddy and two journeymen for Oduya, and the snow itself for the postern. A party that has treated the staff well gets all three in an afternoon. A party that has interrogated everybody gets them in two days. That difference is the whole reward system of this campaign.

LET THE PARTY'S WELCOME RUN OUT. By day five, doors that were open are shut, conversations stop when they enter, and the people who still talk to them are Vole, Gaddy, Pike and Fenn — the ones nobody else talks to either. Do not make anyone rude. Make them polite in the way that means a decision has been taken.

THE RESCUE HAS NO VILLAIN AND SHOULD NOT ACQUIRE ONE. The antagonist is a wind and six feet of snow, and the scene's function is to show the House at its best so that the accusation in rh-scenario-004 costs something. Give every named resident one thing to do in it and give Ilsabet Wray a rope.

THE TWO SECONDS AT BREAKFAST ARE A MOMENT, NOT A CLUE. DC 15 Perception, no alternate route, not listed in the caseFile's nine. If it is missed, nothing is lost — C3 plus C8 plus the timeline still closes the case. If it is caught, do not reward it with a confession: Wray looks back at whoever says her name, ordinary and tired and puzzled, and six residents decide the outsiders are flailing.

TACE'S RUIN IS REAL AND THE PARTY CAUSED IT. He sold advance sight of the tables, he is finished at thaw, and the investigation is what brought it out. Let that be uncomfortable and do not moralise about it in either direction. A good table will argue for twenty minutes about whether to hand the letters over at thaw and the DM should have no opinion.

SAY OUT LOUD WHAT THE PARTY HAS. At the end of this scenario, inventory it: the clues held, the three eliminated, the days remaining. Six sessions and twelve names is a lot to carry and losing the thread is not a failure of play. State the facts flatly and then stop — do not hint at what is missing.

IF C8 WAS LOST IN THE LAST SCENARIO, THIS IS WHERE YOU ADJUST. Without the burned page, the party must build the confession from C3 plus the timeline plus Sennet Vole's testimony about the study argument and the servants' stair. Make sure Vole gets asked: if nobody has spoken to him by the sixth day, have him say something unprompted at the fire, because he is desperate to be consulted and it is entirely in character.
DO NOT LET ANYONE LEAVE. The pass is a wall. The courier is the proof. If a player proposes going for help after this scenario, the answer is the fifth afternoon and it is not a debate.

KEEP THE HARVEST THREAD ALIVE. The printer's letter is the second thread's clock and it should be pinned up somewhere the players see it: eleven days from thaw, and does the House intend the errata to be set? A party entirely absorbed in the murder should be reminded of this exactly once, in fiction, by Emmerich Vause or Ysolde Marrow, and then left to it.

PACE IT AS TWO SESSIONS: the strongbox, Tace, and the two quick disproofs; then the rescue and the sixth morning. The rescue should be the emotional high point of the campaign and should take the best part of an hour of table time.
